passage:
Yamini signed the word for "lunch" and Vaibhav frowned. "That sign means 'meeting' where I learnt," he signed back. "In Chennai we use this one for lunch."
"Really? In Delhi it's this." She showed it slowly.
"Show me again? Or write it." He typed "lunch" on his phone and turned the screen.
She laughed and typed, "Same idea, different hands."
"Which do we use with your cousin?"
"Hers. She's from Delhi too."
He copied the new sign twice, and Yamini corrected the handshape gently. "Good. Your turn. What's your sign for 'tomorrow'?"

qa.q: What did Vaibhav do to check the sign for lunch?
qa.a: He typed "lunch" on his phone and turned the screen.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav thinking when he frowned at Yamini's sign?
qa.a: He was puzzled because the sign meant "meeting" where he learnt it, not lunch.

qa.q: How can signers handle a sign the other does not know?
qa.a: They can show it slowly, write or type it, and agree which sign to use; asking is normal.

qa.q: How might Yamini have felt about the mix-up?
qa.a: She laughed and said "Same idea, different hands," so she seemed amused and unbothered. 🙂

grounding: Signs vary by region, and signers mix signing with typed words; clarifying a sign is normal, not a failure.

passage: I'm Jomon, and I've signed all my life, but moving from Kerala to Delhi showed me how many versions of the same language exist. At my new office Avni, a colleague who was learning Indian Sign Language, signed "thank you" the way her online class had taught it. Mine was different. For a second I didn't follow, and I felt hot, as if I had failed. Then I laughed and showed her mine, and we used a notepad for the rest. Later, when the room was noisy, I mixed signing, lip patterns and a text on my phone. Nobody thought that was odd. Asking someone to repeat a sign wasn't a failure. It just meant we came from different places.

qa.q: What did Jomon and Avni use for the rest of the conversation?
qa.a: A notepad.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling when Jomon did not follow Avni's sign?
qa.a: Jomon felt embarrassed, hot as if he had failed, though later saw it was only a regional difference.

qa.q: What could Avni do when a signer uses a different sign from hers?
qa.a: She can ask them to show theirs and check it, using writing if needed.

qa.q: How might Avni have felt when Jomon laughed and showed a different sign?
qa.a: Probably relieved and glad to learn, since she was learning Indian Sign Language and was not corrected harshly.

grounding: A signer notices regional variation and mixed modes of sign, speech and writing, and treats clarifying a sign as normal.

passage:
Supervisor's note, 5 March. Written by Lakshmi, programme coordinator, Deaf youth centre, Bengaluru.
Anirban joined us this month from Kolkata. He is Deaf and signs Indian Sign Language, as does our senior trainer, Meena, who grew up in Chennai. Today I watched them plan the weekend workshop together. Several times one of them paused, repeated a sign, and the other frowned. Anirban later told me that some everyday signs differ between his city and hers, and that younger and older signers also use different ones. They handled it easily: they fingerspelled the word, wrote it on the whiteboard, or Anirban spoke it aloud while signing, and then agreed which sign to use with the students.
Neither treated this as a mistake. Meena laughed and said, "Now I've learned a Kolkata sign."
Next step: I have asked them to make a short list of the signs they agreed on, to share with the new volunteers.

qa.q: Where did Meena grow up?
qa.a: In Chennai.

qa.q: How did Meena seem to feel about learning a different sign?
qa.a: Meena seemed amused and pleased, laughing that she'd learned a Kolkata sign rather than treating it as a problem.

qa.q: How did Anirban and Meena clarify differing signs?
qa.a: They fingerspelled, wrote on the whiteboard, or Anirban spoke while signing, then agreed which sign to use with the students.

qa.q: What would have changed if Anirban and Meena had treated the differences as mistakes?
qa.a: Planning might have felt tense or embarrassing, instead of the easy, friendly clarifying they did.

grounding: A coordinator notes two signers from different cities meeting regional sign differences and clarifying by mixing fingerspelling, writing and speech.

passage:
Saturday night
Met Ujjwal at the café near the metro today, the Deaf photographer from the community event. I've been learning signs from online videos for three months and was so proud to try them. First thing, I signed what I thought was "coffee". He looked puzzled, then grinned, typed on his phone and showed me: "That's the American sign. Here most people use a different one." Then he showed me his. My face went hot. Three months of practice, and half of it from the wrong country!
But he didn't seem to mind at all. We ended up using everything: his signs, my clumsy ones, typing on the phone, pointing at the menu, a few words on a napkin. He speaks a little too, when he wants to. He told me, "Asking what a sign means is normal. Deaf people do it with each other all the time."
Next week: find a local class, not just videos.
Neelam

qa.q: How long had Neelam been learning signs from online videos?
qa.a: Three months.

qa.q: How did Neelam feel when Ujjwal said the sign was American?
qa.a: Neelam felt embarrassed, face hot, disappointed to have learned signs from another country's sign language.

qa.q: What does Neelam plan to do next, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: Find a local class instead of only videos, so the signs learned match those used by Deaf people nearby.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal see the mix-up?
qa.a: Ujjwal didn't mind at all, grinning and explaining that asking what a sign means is normal, even among Deaf people.

grounding: Shows a learner discovering that signs vary between countries and mixing sign, typing and pointing with a Deaf signer, where clarifying is normal.

passage:
Maria: today's meeting was funny. the Mumbai team used a sign for "deadline" I'd never seen
Rehana: haha which one? Goa and Mumbai signers do some things differently
Maria: I stared at Akash for a whole minute thinking he meant something else entirely 😅
Rehana: oh no. did you ask him?
Maria: eventually. I fingerspelled D-E-A-D-L-I-N-E with a question face and he laughed and nodded
Maria: then the hearing manager started talking and the interpreter used yet another sign 🤦
Rehana: three versions in one meeting lol
Maria: I felt stupid for a moment. like I should know
Rehana: you're not stupid. even interpreters check signs all the time. I ask Deaf clients "which sign do you use?" every week
Maria: really?
Rehana: really. clarifying is part of the language, not a failure
Maria: ok. next time I'll just ask straight away instead of panicking 😊

qa.q: How did Maria finally check the sign?
qa.a: Maria fingerspelled D-E-A-D-L-I-N-E with a question face.

qa.q: How did Maria feel for a moment during the meeting?
qa.a: Maria felt stupid and embarrassed for a moment, feeling the sign should already have been familiar.

qa.q: What does Rehana say about clarifying signs, and why is it helpful?
qa.a: That even interpreters check signs every week, so clarifying is part of the language, which helps Maria ask straight away without shame.

qa.q: How did Akash respond when Maria asked?
qa.a: Akash laughed and nodded, treating the question as perfectly normal.

grounding: Shows a signer meeting regional variation in signs within one meeting and a friend reassuring her that clarifying is normal.

passage:
At the weekly market in Hassan, Harsha's stall sold school uniforms, and her regulars knew to tap the counter to get her attention. On Saturday a young woman, Seema, came up and began signing quickly. Harsha lit up; it had been weeks since she'd met another Deaf signer at the market.
They got along fast, but then Seema made a sign Harsha had never seen, a twist of the hand near her chin, and repeated it, eyebrows raised.
Harsha frowned, shook her head and tried her own guess. Seema shook hers too. They both laughed.
Seema fingerspelled the word slowly, then pulled a pencil from behind her ear and wrote it on the back of a receipt: "hostel." She was from Kolkata, she signed; that was the sign where she had learned.
Harsha showed her the one used at the Deaf club in Hassan. Seema copied it, grinning. Neither treated it as a mistake; just a new word to swap.

qa.q: What word did Seema write on the back of a receipt?
qa.a: She wrote "hostel."

qa.q: How did Harsha feel when Seema began signing?
qa.a: Harsha felt delighted and excited, since it had been weeks since she had met another Deaf signer at the market.

qa.q: What did the two do when a sign didn't match, and why was it a good approach?
qa.a: They laughed, fingerspelled and wrote the word, then swapped their versions, treating the difference as normal rather than a mistake. 🙂

qa.q: Why might Seema's sign have looked unfamiliar to Harsha?
qa.a: Seema learned to sign in Kolkata and Harsha used the sign from the Deaf club in Hassan, so they had different signs for the same word.

grounding: Signers from different regions may use different signs and mix signing with fingerspelling and writing, and clarifying a sign is normal, not a failure.
